## Simple explanation

A token is a piece of text as processed by a language model. A token may
be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or a special control marker;
it is not necessarily the same as a word.

## Technical explanation

Tokenizers map text to discrete token IDs from a model-specific vocabulary.
Subword algorithms such as byte-pair encoding or unigram tokenization
balance vocabulary size and sequence length. Special tokens may mark
boundaries, roles, or tasks.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Tokenization affects context-window usage, inference cost, latency, and
model behavior. Different models tokenize the same text differently, so
token counts and truncation limits are model-dependent.

## How it works

The tokenizer normalizes or segments input text into tokens and maps them
to integer IDs. The model processes those IDs and produces output token
IDs, which the tokenizer decodes back into text.

## Practical example

A long technical term may be split into several subword tokens, while a
common short word may use one token. Before sending a prompt, an application
can count tokens with the target model's tokenizer to avoid exceeding
context limits.

## Common misconceptions

- One token does not always equal one word or one character.
- Token counts are not interchangeable across tokenizers or model
  families.
